news.text: The Trump administration’s latest assertions about executive privilege — that it protects the confidentiality of a president’s communication with private advisers who aren’t part of the government — are like too much else in this White House: politically unprecedented, legally wrong and morally dubious.From a legal standpoint, the point of executive privilege is to protect communications that occur within the government, between the president and other public officials. news.title: CIA Chief Warned Putin Against NATO Attack During Surprise Moscow Visit – Reports
news.text:
CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise trip to Moscow on Tuesday to warn Russian President Vladimir Putin against attacking a NATO member, amid the Kremlin’s stalled war against Ukraine, The Wall Street Journal and Politico reported on Aug. 26, citing sources familiar with the matter.

The warnings reportedly focused on Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania – the three Baltic NATO members that border Russia.

The US intelligence community has previously assessed that Moscow could seek to “test NATO’s resolve” with a limited attack on an alliance member, according to the WSJ. US officials reportedly believe such an attack could involve a cyberattack or a small-scale ground incursion into one of the Baltic states.

The assessment comes as Russia’s war against Ukraine continues to consume Western ammunition stocks, potentially creating vulnerabilities that Moscow could seek to exploit, according to WSJ sources.

Ratcliffe also warned Putin against providing military and economic support to Iran, Politico reported.

Neither Washington nor Moscow has publicly disclosed the results of Ratcliffe’s visit.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Putin did not meet with Ratcliffe and that the CIA chief’s contacts in Moscow were conducted at the intelligence-services level.

US President Donald Trump described the trip as “partly routine.”

After returning to Washington, however, Ratcliffe attended a closed-door meeting between Trump and senior US national security officials, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Gen. Dan Caine, chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The meeting lasted about three hours.

Ratcliffe’s visit echoes a similar trip by then-CIA Director William Burns to Moscow in November 2021, just months before Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

Burns met with senior Russian officials, including then-Security Council Secretary Nikolai Patrushev and Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin. He also spoke with Putin by phone.

According to CNN, Burns warned Moscow about the consequences of its troop movements near Ukraine and stressed that an invasion would be unacceptable.

Putin ultimately launched the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.

Washington asked Kyiv to hold fire

Ahead of Ratcliffe’s trip, Washington asked Ukraine to temporarily suspend strikes on Russian territory while the US delegation was in Moscow.

Axios reported that the US told Kyiv a senior delegation was traveling to Moscow and asked Ukraine to pause strikes until it had left.

Ukrainian government sources later confirmed to public broadcaster Suspilne that Washington specifically asked Kyiv not to strike Moscow and St. Petersburg during the visit.

The request came as Ukrainian forces have increasingly carried out long-range strikes against targets deep inside Russia, including in the Moscow region.
news.summary: CIA Director John Ratcliffe secretly traveled to Moscow this week to warn Vladimir Putin against attacking NATO, The Wall Street Journal and Politico reported. The warning reportedly focused on the Baltic states, amid US intelligence concerns that Russia could seek to “test NATO’s resolve” with a limited attack.

news.title: Donald Trump Mocked Online For Declaring 'Mission Accomplished' In Iran

Trump’s claim comes despite the fact that there is still no sign of a peace deal to end the Iran conflict.

news.title: Trump-Iran war at six months: goals shift, Hormuz remains shut, no end in sight
news.text: Six months after President Donald Trump launched the war with Iran in late February, there is still no clear way out, despite his repeated claims that the war has been won or that a deal is close. Trump had initially said the conflict would last four to five weeks, but a June memorandum of understanding meant to help end it has since fallen away.As the conflict has stretched on, the US has seen stockpiles of key weapons diminish and has shifted more towards economic pressure on Iran rather than fresh strikes. The war’s aims have also changed, with reopening the Strait of Hormuz now a central goal, even though it was not among Trump’s original objectives.The strait had been a vital shipping route through which about 20% of the world’s oil passed. Since the war began, it has been largely closed after Iran turned it into a chokepoint for the global economy, pushing up prices of fuel and fertiliser and adding economic and political pressure in the US.The US has had tactical success in damaging Iran’s military capabilities, but several objectives set out by Trump at the start of the war remain unmet, while others have shifted over time.On Iran’s nuclear programme, Trump said last June that the US had “obliterated” it. But when the war began, his aides had argued that Iran was only weeks away from developing a bomb. One of the main unresolved questions is what will happen to about 970 pounds, or 440 kilograms, of enriched uranium that Tehran could potentially use for a weapon. The material is believed to be buried under three sites bombed by the US and Israel last year.In a social media post on May 29, Trump said the uranium would be retrieved by the US “in close coordination and conjunction with the Islamic Republic of Iran, plus the International Atomic Energy Agency, and DESTROYED”. Iran has not said whether it would agree. Experts have said that, without Iran’s permission, taking it would be a dangerous mission that would require a sizable deployment of US troops into the country.Officials said Tehran reaffirmed in the June memorandum of understanding that it would not procure or develop nuclear weapons. The deal also called for Iran to dilute its stockpile of highly enriched uranium. But many other details were left for future talks, and it is unclear how much progress was made before negotiations quickly broke down.On the Strait of Hormuz, Trump has said a proposed deal with Iran would reopen the waterway and lead the US to end its blockade of Tehran’s ports. At other times, he has suggested the strait would somehow become American territory and that the US could charge a toll on passing ships.Trump has also repeatedly said the strait is open. In an interview on Wednesday on conservative commentator Glenn Beck’s radio show, he said: “It’s a functioning strait. Yes, every once in a while, there’ll be a drone or a rocket or something shot, but it is a very functioning strait.”Another stated objective was to “destroy their missiles and raze their missile industry to the ground”. In late March, Trump said Iran’s missiles were “mostly decimated” and that 90% of its missiles and launchers had been knocked out. By mid-May, he gave a lower estimate, saying 82% of Iran’s missiles were gone.Iran, however, has continued to show that it can launch attacks in the region, including drone strikes on ships passing through the strait. As recently as July, the US military was still striking Iranian targets. US Central Command said those attacks were aimed at “Iranian military command centres, air defence and coastal surveillance sites, maritime capabilities, missile and drone launch sites and communications networks”.The destruction of Iran’s defence industrial base was sometimes presented early in the war as a separate objective, though it later appeared less often in official messaging. US Central Command has said its targets included weapons production facilities and missile and drone manufacturing sites. Secretary of State Marco Rubio told lawmakers in early June that Iran had suffered “massive destruction” to its defence industrial base and “80 to 90% of attrition. It will take years for them to rebuild it.”On Iran’s navy and air force, the US and Israel quickly established air superiority over Iran and operated there with little resistance. Rubio told lawmakers that Iran still has drone capabilities, but no longer has the ability to carry out swarm attacks as it did at the start of the war. He also said Iran no longer has a navy and now relies on small boats fitted with machine guns that harass ships and sometimes drop mines in the water. Trump said on Wednesday that Iran’s navy and air force are “totally gone”.Trump later added another goal in a March social media post: “Protecting, at the highest level, our Middle Eastern Allies, including Israel, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, the United Arab Emirates, Bahrain, Kuwait, and others.” The US keeps thousands of troops at bases and other sites in the region, but Trump has not made clear how far he is prepared to go in the long term to defend those allies.In June, after the US said Iran had fired missiles at Kuwait and Bahrain, Washington responded with strikes on Iran. But Oman has stood apart from the other allies mentioned by Trump. It has instead faced his anger over the deal it was negotiating with Iran on the Strait of Hormuz. In mid-August, Trump threatened in an interview that the US would bomb Oman if it “gets in the way”, using an expletive for emphasis.Cutting off support for Iranian proxy groups was also repeatedly described by Trump and his administration in March as a key objective. Over time, officials have offered fewer updates on that goal, which Trump described as ensuring that “the region’s terrorist proxies can no longer destabilize the region or the world and attack our forces” and “ensuring that the Iranian regime cannot continue to arm, fund, and direct terrorist armies outside of their borders”.Early in the conflict, the US struck Iranian-aligned militia groups in Iraq. But the biggest focus has been Israel’s war in Lebanon against the Iran-backed Hezbollah. Iran has said that the fighting in Lebanon must stop as part of any deal with the US. Israel and the Lebanese government later announced a US-mediated agreement under which Israeli forces would leave southern Lebanon in exchange for Hezbollah’s disarmament. An administration official, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment on the record, described that as a “huge step”. Hezbollah, however, has refused direct talks, and its leader has said the group will not disarm.Six months into the war, the US says it has badly damaged Iran’s military strength, but several of the aims set out at the start remain unresolved. With the June understanding no longer in play and the conflict’s goals continuing to shift, there is still no clear end in sight.With PTI Inputs- EndsPublished By: India Today Web Desk Published On: Aug 27, 2026 11:28 IST

news.title: Miley Cyrus remembers ‘angel’ godmother Dolly Parton after death at 80
news.text:
Miley Cyrus has led tributes to her “angel” godmother Dolly Parton after the death of he country music superstar at the age of 80, following a “brief battle with cancer”.

Wrecking Ball singer Cyrus, 33, frequently cited the queen of country as a deeply meaningful figure in her life.

She wrote on Instagram: “The feeling of losing my Aunt Dolly is beyond what feels right to share. Our most sacred moments were private and they’ll stay there behind the stage, beneath the glamour & between our hearts.

“What I know is Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong. I have an angel by my side. I always have. One of our last conversations was about music and metamorphosis.

“I will always love her and want to make her proud. My heart breaks for the world, her family and friends who will miss her deeply. We’re in this loss together and we will see her in all of the most beautiful things.”

Parton played Aunt Dolly on Cyrus’s breakout TV show, Hannah Montana.

They also performed a number of duets together including a cover of Wrecking Ball for Parton’s 2023 rock album Rockstar.

Cyrus join the biggest names in music, including: Sir Elton John, Sir Paul McCartney, Sir Mick Jagger, Taylor Swift and Beyonce; in detailing her impact and her legacy, as both a musician and a humanitarian.

The Band of the Coldstream Guards played 9 To 5, one of her biggest hits, on the forecourt of Buckingham Palace during Changing the Guard on Wednesday.

Meanwhile, landmarks around the US were lit up pink in her honour, including the Empire State Building in New York, the Willis Tower in Chicago and the Pacific Park Ferris Wheel in Los Angeles.

News of Parton’s death was announced by her family on Tuesday night, and her publicist, Marcel Pariseau, said: “After bravely facing a brief battle with cancer, Dolly departed her earthly life today at the Vanderbilt-Ingram Cancer Centre surrounded by loved ones.”

The singer was best known for her genre-defining hits including 9 To 5, I Will Always Love You and Jolene.

The statement continued: “Our beloved Dolly Parton spent her life and career bringing joy, laughter, hope and integrity into everything she touched. Her unmatched generosity reached the lives of countless people whom she would never meet, yet she was always there to offer a helping hand.

“Whether it be the hundreds of millions of books donated through her invaluable Imagination Library or funding research that helped create a lifesaving vaccine used around the world, Dolly’s unconditional love for all people was the guiding force for her lasting impact.”

The type of cancer was not disclosed.

Parton’s death was announced late on Tuesday via an Instagram video by her nephew, Bryan Seaver, who also served as the singer’s head of security.

He said it was “an honour that is mixed with absolute pride and great sadness” to share the news of her death, adding: “But sadness lies with us, not with Dolly.

“Dolly has lived in the light and is in the arms of Jesus, surely met by Carl, her parents and countless others who have watched her and longed to meet her in the heavens.”

Parton’s husband Carl Dean died last year aged 82.

Flags will be lowered throughout America in Parton’s honour, US President Donald Trump announced, posting on Truth Social “there has never been anyone like her”.

Jane Fonda, who starred in the film 9 To 5 with Parton and was a lifelong friend, said she was “devastated”, adding: “I know that millions are mourning and I want to say this – more than anyone I have ever known, Dolly will always be with us because she was so present, so powerful, so generous and playful that she is woven into all our lives and hearts forever.

“We have our memories of her, her songs, Dollywood, ‘9 to 5′, the millions of books she got into the hands of children, all the iconic images that bring her to us.

“And they are all blessings. Let’s be grateful for all that she has left us to ease our sadness now.”

The Bee Gees’ Barry Gibb, who co-wrote Islands In The Stream for Parton and Kenny Rogers, wrote in a tribute on X: “Dolly was next to me at the microphone, and we were reminiscing about when we made Islands in the Stream, among other memories.

“She suddenly turned to me and said, ‘Where we are standing right now is where I wrote Jolene, and I Will Always Love You.'”

“This is how I remember Dolly, a gigantic talent possessed by an artist who was unreachable,” he added.

“Her songs were the greatest, and she was the greatest; no matter what, she will live on. Whenever she entered a room, she sparkled, and I believe she always will.”

Sir Elton said he was “shocked and devastated” to hear of her death, adding she was “a giant of an artist – unique and irreplaceable, with the kindest heart”.

She added: “Dolly, you were the barometer. The north star. Bold and brilliant. Talented and tenacious. You taught so many lessons on how to be uniquely oneself. I am grateful for your art, your heart, your generosity, your humour, your entrepreneurship.

“I’m honoured that I had the privilege to work with you. I will treasure that forever. Thank you for your profound impact on the world. You are an angel who has made this world a happier place because of your joyful art. You are truly one of one. Rest peacefully.”

Swift said a world without Dolly Parton “doesn’t feel possible, real, or right”.

She added: “But because of the eternally generous way she spent her time on this earth and the countless lives she changed for the better, her legacy will be an everlasting one.

“She was truly the gift that kept on giving. Dolly gave us someone to look up to while encouraging us to be who we are as individuals. Somehow, she was able to give us her lessons about the world gently and honestly, simultaneously, and oftentimes hilariously.”

Sir Paul remembered Parton as a “magnificent star”, adding: “It is hard to imagine living in a world without Dolly”, while Sir Mick said: “We will all miss her so much.”

Piano Man singer Billy Joel said Parton “transcended time and became one of those iconic artists who is known for just being Dolly, beyond a specific song or moment in time”.

Talk show host Oprah Winfrey said “she brought the light, and we are all better because she was here”.

The family of country singer Kenny Rogers, with whom Parton duetted on Islands In The Stream, said: “It’s painstakingly hard to put into words what you meant to Kenny… and to all of us.

“When the two of you sang about being islands in the stream who together had found peace unknown, having real love for each other as true friends who would always stand by each other, and how you just can’t make old friends, it was always as genuine as it could possibly be… coming straight from the heart and reflecting what you both felt for each other.”

Rogers died in 2020.

In May, Parton pulled out of a highly anticipated Las Vegas residency, which was due to begin in September.

She had already postponed her six-date run at the Colosseum Theatre at Caesars Palace from December 2025 to deal with “health challenges”.

At Parton’s request, a small, private funeral service will be held for immediate family, a statement from her family on social media said.

In lieu of flowers, her family asked for donations to be made to Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library.

She was a savvy businesswoman with an empire that included a theme park, aptly named Dollywood, and a pioneering philanthropist.

Imagination Library, a programme devoted to inspiring a love of reading in children, has given more than 300 million books to youngsters.

She was also a supporter of several charities for black and LGBT+ communities, as well as the Barbara Davis Centre for Childhood Diabetes, Save the Music Foundation and the Boot Campaign.

In 2020, she donated one million dollars (£733,000) to coronavirus research at Vanderbilt University, which helped fund Moderna’s Covid-19 vaccine.

Parton was also a prolific songwriter, who penned I Will Always Love You – one of the defining love songs of the 20th century – as a goodbye to her former creative partner, Porter Wagoner, who hired her to be his sidekick on his eponymous TV show and helped her land a record deal.

The song became a blockbuster hit when Whitney Houston recorded a cover for the 1992 film, The Bodyguard.

Parton was born in a single-room cabin in Locust Ridge, Tennessee, in 1946, the fourth of 12 children.

She began her musical journey at the age of six, singing in the local church where her grandfather was the pastor.

By the age of 13, she had reached the pinnacle of country music success: an appearance at the Grand Ole Opry in Nashville, Tennessee.

Over the course of her career, which spanned more than 60 years, Parton sold more than 100 million records worldwide and wrote more than 3,000 songs, including hits Coat Of Many Colours and Joshua.
news.summary: The queen of country was a deeply significant figure in her life.
news.author: Laura Harding

news.title: Appeals court allows charges against Rep. LaMonica McIver to proceed
news.text:
Aug. 27 (UPI) -- A divided federal appeals court has ruled that Rep. LaMonica McIver is not immune from prosecution on charges stemming from a confrontation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents outside a federal immigration detention facility in 2025.

The New Jersey Democrat was charged with three federal counts of impeding and interfering with federal immigration officers over alleged conduct on May 9, 2025, as they were attempting to arrest Newark Mayor Ras Baraka during an unannounced congressional oversight inspection of Delaney Hall Federal Immigration Facility.

McIver denies the allegations and has sought their dismissal.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled 2-1 Wednesday that two of the three charges against McIver may proceed to trial, while the third was sent back to a lower court for reconsideration.

McIver said she disagrees with the ruling and was "exploring" her options.

"To protect the people, their elected representatives must be authorized to conduct oversight of the executive branch without fear of retaliation," McIver said in a statement.

"Today's decision chills that authority and emboldens the Trump administration to continue persecuting our most vulnerable communities, those who try to defend them and anyone who dares hold the president or his lackeys accountable.

"I will not fold to this administration," she continued. "The administration will not stop me from doing my job or standing for what is right. This is not over."

Federal prosecutors charged McIver in a three-count indictment in June 2025, a month after the incident at Delaney Hall.

According to the court document, she and two other members of Congress were at the facility to conduct an unannounced congressional oversight inspection of the facility as a protest was occurring outside against the Trump administration's hardline immigration policy and Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

After arriving at the facility, Baraka entered but was informed by a federal officer he was not authorized to be there, according to federal prosecutors, who said McIver prevented the federal officers from arresting the mayor, who was allegedly given multiple warnings to leave.

Outside the facility, McIver allegedly placed herself in front of Baraka and wrapped her arms around him to prevent his arrest. During the situation she is accused of having "slammed her forearm into the body of one law enforcement officer," whom she also allegedly tried to retrain by grabbing him.

Court documents also accuse her of striking a second officer with both of her forearms.

Video of the incident posted online shows a chaotic scene that day outside the facility.

Baraka was eventually arrested and charged with trespassing, though the case against him was later dropped.

McIver moved to dismiss the indictment, arguing it violated the Speech or Debate Clause and the constitutional principle of separation of powers as well as under selective prosecution and enforcement claims, while also arguing selective and vindictive prosecution and enforcement.

All three counts accuse her of forcibly assaulting, resisting, opposing, impeding, intimidating and interfering with federal officers. However, the appeals court sent count three back to the lower court to review whether it includes conduct that can be considered legislative acts.

While counts one and two identify specifics act, count three encompasses a range of alleged conduct over a broad time frame, both inside and outside the facility, the court said.

Numerous Democrats came to McIver's defense, arguing it is an attack on congressional oversight.

"Donald Trump wants Congressmembers to fall in line & not conduct oversight of detention centers," Rep. Ayanna Pressley of Massachusetts said in a statement.

"And he wants to make an example out of @RepLaMonica. But we're not letting up."

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill similarly said that she continues to stand with her friend.

"Trump weaponizing the Department of Justice to target members of Congress simply for doing their jobs is straight out of his corruption playbook," she said in an online statement.

"It's a brazen and unlawful abuse of power, and a direct attack on congressional oversight."
news.summary: A federal appeals court has ruled that Rep. LaMonica McIver is not immune from prosecution on charges stemming from a confrontation with ICE agents.

news.text: Shares of Indian power equipment manufacturers, including CG Power, GE Vernova, Hitachi Energy India and Transformers and Rectifiers (India), gained in Thursday’s trading session after US President Donald Trump announced measures targeting certain foreign-made equipment used in the country’s electricity grid.CG Power led the gains among the sector’s stocks, climbing as much as 4%, while GE Vernova rose around 3%. news.title: Jelly Roll breaks silence over ‘weirdest’ Trump joke he made
news.text:
Jelly Roll didn't back down after backlash to a joke he made referring to President Donald Trump as a “fat pig” while serving as guest host of Jimmy Kimmel Live! this week.

The three-time Grammy winner addressed all the criticism from people who said he was essentially insulting his own audience after taking shots at Trump's weight during his monologue.

He said he was surprised that the remarks were “the weirdest thing I've ever done to stun people,” describing himself as a “former felon; a drug dealer who has lost 300 pounds;” and a person who has “tattoos all over his face.”

Jelly Roll, whose full name is Jason Bradley DeFord, added, “What a turn of events: Who would have guessed I'd get in more trouble with the president than Rosie O'Donnell?”

The Save Me vocalist said he felt that Trump should have thicker skin being in the Oval Office.

“Let's be honest for a second - any U.S. president should be able to handle a few jokes, right?” Jelly Roll said. “They should also be able to handle gas prices, healthcare and the occasional international conflict, but beggars can't be choosers.”

The country music star raised eyebrows on Monday after directing punchlines in the president's direction when speaking about the IndyCar Freedom 250 event in Washington, D.C.

Jelly Roll joked that “the president seemed to enjoy the IndyCar race, which was a real switch-up for him because normally he only likes his own race.”

“Trump also drove around the track in his motorcade doing what they call the ‘lap of honor’ - which sounds like a loyalty program at a strip club.”

He then shifted the topic to Trump's appearance, saying that the Sunday drive marked “the only laps Trump's been doing lately.”

After a montage of clips of Trump alluding to people's appearances, Jelly Roll said, “Well, Mr. President, from one fat pig to another, take it from me that physical fitness is very important.”

“It’s crazy, think about this, y’all. In the last few years, I’ve lost 300 pounds. That means I’ve lost an entire Donald Trump - and let’s be honest, based on his approval ratings, it seems like most of the country wants to do the same thing,” he concluded as his jokes on Donald Trump received mixed reviews.

news.title: Canada is bolstering its defense industry as US relations fray. A boom is on for local contractors
news.text:
APCanada is bolstering its defense industry as US relations fray

TORONTO: As Canada moves to reduce its dependence on American military suppliers, the push is on display inside a Toronto garment factory.Hunched over sewing machines, two workers rapidly stitch together pieces of camouflage-patterned fabric and Velcro strips. In the next room, workers snip stray threads as they inspect the finished product: helmet covers for the Canadian military.The factory is assembling uniforms for Wuxly, a luxury parka maker that is among a flurry of Canadian companies branching into defense contracting. As Canadian military spending surges, others are developing remote sensors for the country's vast Arctic region, making drones to resupply soldiers, and building autonomous robots.The boom in the defense sector reflects Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's vow to strengthen the country's economic self-sufficiency amid fraying relations with Washington, including a fresh escalation this week with new rounds of tariffs.Canadian startups and established companies, alongside firms in Europe, are set to benefit from tens of billions of dollars in extra defense funding, driven partly by pressure from U.S. President Donald Trump to contribute more to NATO. Canada's investment remains small compared with the Pentagon's budget, but its strategy aims to boost domestic defense capabilities, and not just U.S. contractors.Live EventsA country known for peacekeeping ramps up military spendingA defense industrial strategy released earlier this year by Carney represents a generational shift for Canada, which invented modern peacekeeping and had long been content to remain in the shadow of its southern neighbor on defense matters.The defense plan earmarks an additional $60 billion in funding over the next five years, and the government has promised support for domestic businesses to sell into defense and security supply chains. Currently, Canada spends about $36 billion to $43 billion on national defense."The scale of investment that is involved is quite significant by Canadian standards, certainly in peacetime," said Philippe Lagasse, an associate professor at Carleton University specializing in defense policy.The defense boom is "quite evident at all the events we're at. Every defense show (is) sold out. Lots of new companies and (other) industries coming into the (defense) industry, getting involved," said Wuxly founder and CEO James Yurichuk.Wuxly's helmet covers, destined for the Canadian Armed Forces, allow soldiers to attach call sign patches or gear like lights, cameras and beacons. The company also makes military parkas and tank covers and has been supplying Ukraine's military with gear, including 40,000 female uniforms - one of the company's specialties.Carney has called for upgrading the Canadian military's Arctic capabilities, increasing spending by tens of billions of dollars to assert sovereignty over the vast but sparsely populated and increasingly contested region."There's a lot of innovation that can create advantage in the North, and with the Arctic region being so important, we've got to clothe our soldiers properly," Yurichuk said.Canadian companies and European allies find new opportunitiesA major part of the strategy is diversifying away from U.S. defense contractors. It focuses on tapping a wider global pool of suppliers of military hardware - and fostering domestic defense supply chains.The strategy envisions investments amounting to more than half a trillion dollars, creating 125,000 jobs and tripling the size of the country's defense industry over the next decade by steering contracts to Canadian companies. It calls for accelerating research and development and prioritizes developing key "sovereign capabilities" including aerospace, robotics and unmanned systems.As Canada pursues partnerships with other allies, in addition to the United States, Ottawa has announced deals this year to buy radar planes from Sweden's Saab over American competitors and submarines from Germany's ThyssenKrupp.Canadian startups like New Frontier Robotics also are lining up to play a part."There definitely is money in play," said Nikhil Malhotra, co-founder of the two-person company. "We see it. Obviously, we are going for it."The company is working on a mobile manipulator robot - essentially a robot arm on a mobile platform - powered by artificial intelligence that could have both military and civilian applications, in what's known as dual-use technology.The initial plan was to target manufacturing, with robots working autonomously between assembly lines, but potential customers suggested there was also a growing need from the defense industry. Robots could also be used for support roles at military bases, Malhotra said."If you have infrastructure up in the Arctic that needs maintenance, obviously the climate is very dangerous. Are you really willing to risk an operator's life? The answer is no. It's better to put this thing on," said Malhotra, whose company is based temporarily at a robotics lab at the University of Waterloo, about 60 miles (100 kilometers) west of Toronto.Startups focus on products with versatilityCanada's efforts to modernize its war machine still face big potential challenges, including the risk that opposition parties target Carney's spending plans in future elections.Companies that develop novel technologies could be lured to the U.S. by its much larger defense market. It also will be tough for Canadian companies competing against American counterparts with much bigger research and development budgets that mean they are "always going to be a bit more at the edge of the technological capability," Lagasse said.Still, the strategy opens new possibilities for companies like drone maker Volatus Aerospace, based near Montreal."Defense was not a popular topic for a small-cap Canadian public company in the past," CEO Glen Lynch said.Lynch said Canada has had limited manufacturing capability not just for drones "but manufacturing capability in general."Like New Frontier, Volatus' technology is considered dual use. Because Canada is technically not at war, companies can't rely on selling exclusively to the military.Volatus makes drones and related services for civilian and commercial uses, such as air dropping medicine to isolated communities. But it also has a defense unit and makes first-person-view drones, also known as kamikaze drones, which take out targets by crashing into them.The company does some testing at a 100-acre site north of Toronto accessed by an unmarked gravel road and surrounded by fields of corn. Volatus employees demonstrated several aircraft on a recent visit by The Associated Press.The company showed off a drone with a 60-kilogram (132-pound) payload slung underneath by cable, and a scaled-down drone with tilt-wing rotors that can carry cargo over long distances. In a demonstration, the drones operated autonomously and flew in a circular pattern before landing.One drone, dubbed the Canary, has payload bay doors and is used to airdrop medical supplies to remote indigenous First Nations communities in Alberta.It could also be used to send "resupply packages for soldiers" as well as dropping munitions, said Chief Operations Officer Greg Colacitti.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Totalni rat Kanade i SAD-a: Građani bojkotiraju američke proizvode, stižu i nove carine
news.text:
Eskalacija trgovinskog rata sa Sjedinjenim Državama potaknula je val ekonomskog patriotizma u Kanadi, gdje vlada sve otvorenije poziva građane da kupuju domaće proizvode dok se odnosi s najvećim trgovinskim partnerom dodatno pogoršavaju.

Nakon novih američkih carina, Kanada je pojačala kampanju usmjerenu na kupnju domaćih proizvoda, a dio potrošača već dulje izbjegava američku robu. Posebno je izražen bojkot američkog alkohola, koji su kanadske pokrajine povukle s polica.

„Korisno je prisjetiti se da je najveća moć koju posjedujemo naša vlastita kupovna moć. Možemo i moramo birati kupovati kanadsko“, rekao je u utorak ministar financija François-Philippe Champagne prilikom predstavljanja kanadskog odgovora na nove američke carine.

„Kada odaberete kanadski proizvod, osim što vršite pritisak na SAD, štitite radna mjesta u Kanadi“, poručila je ministrica industrije Mélanie Joly.

Promjena ponašanja potrošača vidljiva je i u trgovinama. Oko 40 posto kanadskih kupaca namirnica, prema nedavnom istraživanju, aktivno provjerava podrijetlo proizvoda kako bi izbjeglo robu proizvedenu u SAD-u.

U trgovinama se zato sve češće mogu vidjeti oznake s javorovim listom, kojima se ističe kanadsko podrijetlo proizvoda. Trgovački lanci također koriste gospodarski patriotizam u marketinškim kampanjama.

Bojkot američke robe traje mjesecima

Bojkot se posebno snažno proširio na američka alkoholna pića. Američko vino, pivo i žestoka pića u većini kanadskih pokrajina više nisu na policama, dok su Saskatchewan i Alberta ostale među rijetkim iznimkama. Saskatchewan je ovaj tjedan čak najavio 50-postotnu carinu na američki alkohol od 8. rujna.

Bojkot se prelio i na turizam, iako najnoviji podaci pokazuju da se putovanja Kanađana prema SAD-u počinju oporavljati.

U 2025. broj povratnih putovanja kanadskih stanovnika iz SAD-a pao je 25,4 posto, na 29,1 milijun, dok su u lipnju 2026. Kanađani ostvarili 2,3 milijuna povratnih putovanja iz SAD-a, pet posto više nego godinu ranije. Ipak, njihov je broj i dalje bio 24,6 posto manji nego u lipnju 2024.

To pokazuje da turistički bojkot nije nestao, ali više nije jednako snažan kao tijekom prošle godine.

Kanada uvodi nove carine

Sukob između dviju zemalja u međuvremenu je prerastao bojkot proizvoda i turističkih putovanja.

Sjedinjene Države su od 22. kolovoza uvele nove carine od 50 posto na kanadsku robu vrijednu 27,6 milijardi dolara. Kanada je odgovorila protumjerama koje stupaju na snagu 8. rujna.

Ottawa će uvesti carine od 15, 25 i 50 posto, ovisno o odgovarajućoj američkoj stopi. Mjere će obuhvatiti robu vrijednu 27,6 milijardi dolara, a među najpogođenijim sektorima bit će čelik, mliječni proizvodi, kućanski uređaji, poljoprivredna oprema, celuloza i papir te elektronika.

Kanadska vlada pritom je poručila da će izjednačiti nove američke carine dolar za dolar i stopu za stopu, kako bi zaštitila domaće proizvođače.

Ottawa pripremila 7,5 milijardi dolara pomoći

Paralelno s protumjerama, Kanada je objavila paket novih i proširenih mjera vrijedan 7,5 milijardi kanadskih dolara za pomoć radnicima i poduzećima pogođenima američkim carinama.

Paket uključuje dodatnih 1,5 milijardi dolara za pomoć malim i srednjim poduzećima, 500 milijuna dolara nove likvidnosne potpore, dvije milijarde dolara kroz novi fond za diversifikaciju gospodarstva te 3,5 milijardi dolara za brzu pomoć radnicima i poslodavcima.

Ottawa istodobno pokušava smanjiti ovisnost o američkom tržištu, potaknuti trgovinu unutar Kanade i pronaći nova izvozna tržišta.

Trump najavljuje novo zaoštravanje

Washington zasad ne pokazuje znakove popuštanja. Donald Trump je nakon propasti trgovinskih pregovora poručio da je vrijeme da se Kanadi pokaže da se „ovo više ne može raditi“, dok je dodatno zaprijetio 50-postotnim carinama na kanadske automobile, kamione i autodijelove od 1. siječnja 2027.

Automobilska industrija posebno je osjetljiva jer su proizvodni lanci Kanade i SAD-a desetljećima duboko povezani. Nove carine zato bi mogle pogoditi obje strane granice, a ne samo kanadske proizvođače.

Riječ je o dvjema gospodarstvima koja su iznimno povezana. Kanada je važan dobavljač energije i sirovina za SAD, dok američke kompanije ovise o kanadskim sirovinama i dijelovima za industriju.

Zbog toga trgovinski sukob sve više mijenja i ponašanje kanadskih potrošača. Bojkot američke robe, povlačenje američkog alkohola s polica, slabiji odlazak u SAD, nove carine i milijarde dolara državne pomoći pokazuju da spor više nije samo pitanje trgovinske politike.

Kanadska vlada sada otvoreno poziva građane da „kupuju kanadsko“, dok paralelno pokušava ojačati domaće gospodarstvo i diversificirati trgovinske odnose.
news.summary: Kanađani sve više okreću leđa američkoj robi, a Ottawa otvoreno poziva građane da kupuju domaće proizvode.

news.title: Republicans Quietly Cut Dolly Parton's Reading Programme Months Before Trump Lowered Flags in Her Honour
news.text: Donald Trump ordered US flags lowered nationwide within hours of Dolly Parton's death, calling it 'a true loss for millions of people'. Yet Republican lawmakers in two states had quietly cut funding for her flagship children's reading programme months earlier.A Nation Mourns as Flags FallTrump announced the tribute on Truth Social hours after Parton's family confirmed her death on 25 August. 'There has never been anyone like her, and never will,' he wrote, ordering the American flag lowered for a week beginning that evening.The presidential proclamation directs flags at all federal buildings, military bases, and US embassies to fly at half-staff until sunset on 1 September. Parton spent decades avoiding party politics and turned down the Presidential Medal of Freedom three times, twice under Trump.She died in Nashville at 80 after what her publicist, Marcel Pariseau, described as a brief battle with cancer.Missouri Froze Enrolment Weeks Before Her DeathThe public mourning sits awkwardly beside decisions made in Republican-controlled statehouses. Missouri's fiscal year 2027 budget cut funding for Parton's Imagination Library from roughly $6 million (£4.4 million) to about $2 million (£1.5 million), forcing the state to stop accepting new applicants from 1 July.The Missouri Department of Elementary and Secondary Education said 161,361 children were enrolled when the freeze took effect. Those already signed up will keep receiving books only while the reduced funding lasts.Families with newborns can no longer join, and the department said it was unsure whether the programme would survive as a state-funded effort. The programme has warned its remaining money could run out within four to six months. Missouri had become the first state to fully fund the library in 2024.Indiana Dropped Its Match a Year EarlierIndiana went further. State lawmakers removed the program entirely from the 2025 budget, ending a matching arrangement that had helped reach more than 125,000 children across every county.The state had previously committed a $6 million, two-year allocation under former governor Eric Holcomb, and the programme was credited with lifting Indiana's child literacy ranking from 19th to sixth.His successor, Governor Mike Braun, said Indiana would look to private donations to replace the roughly $3 million (£2.2 million) a year the state had provided. Democratic representative Maureen Bauer called the removal 'a disservice' and said her party would try to restore the money.A Programme That Reaches MillionsParton founded the Imagination Library in 1995 as a tribute to her father, who could not read or write. The charity has posted more than 300 million free books to children and serves over three million youngsters across the US, UK, Canada, Australia, and Ireland.The Dollywood Foundation, which runs the programme, said it would carry on. 'The work ahead has never felt more meaningful, and we will carry it forward,' it wrote hours after her death. Jeff Conyers, the foundation's president, had earlier urged Braun and Indiana legislators to restore funding, arguing the programme 'unites us all, regardless of politics'.Donations have climbed nationwide since Parton died, offering a lifeline as the charity works to keep books arriving in mailboxes the states will no longer pay for.For the parents of enrolled children, whether those deliveries continue now depends on fundraising rather than public money.

news.title: Pentagon's NATO review preparing troop options for Hegseth by November 6
news.text:
ReutersThe Pentagon building in Arlington, Virginia, US 

Washington: A Pentagon review of US troop deployments in Europe will create at least four sets of options for Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth by November 6, well ahead of a December deadline for the review's completion, according to a document seen by Reuters.NATO allies worry that the six-month review, announced in June, will lead to large-scale cuts to the roughly ​80,000 US forces across Europe and punish countries that President Donald Trump believes failed to support the US-Israeli war against Iran.The Pentagon's "Terms of Reference," which have not been previously detailed, explain the steps that the internal review will take and some of the criteria that will be used to evaluate US basing decisions throughout Europe.Also Read: China seeks public tips on procurement violations in elite Rocket ForceOne important disclosure in the document is a plan for the top US general in ‌Europe to participate in a ⁠decision briefing ⁠with the Pentagon's policy chief, Elbridge Colby, by September 18, according to the document.Live EventsThat briefing will be key, according to the document, in hashing out options to develop for Hegseth.NATO skepticism of US review processColby is expected to ​speak with NATO ambassadors about the review on Thursday at the alliance's Brussels headquarters.Asked about the Terms of Reference, a senior Pentagon official said the fact that a spectrum of options would ​be generated, in detail, underscored the seriousness of the process."We want to be able to talk through the pros and cons of a variety of different force levels or dispositions," the official told Reuters.Also Read: Bangladesh in talks to buy Chinese J-10CE fighter jetsIt is unclear, however, whether the details will convince European officials skeptical of the review process, who say privately they are concerned Washington's decision is all but ​made.The Trump administration has long signaled it intends to reduce the military resources it devotes to Europe, with the expectation ⁠that NATO ‌allies will carry a greater share of the burden than they have historically.Trump has also fumed that European NATO allies have long relied on US security guarantees while providing inadequate support for the Iran war. Accusations include that some allies failed to grant basing and overflight access to US warplanes, or ⁠did it too slowly.NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte has expressed some understanding of Trump's disappointment but said ​the large majority of Europeans have been helpful.The Pentagon official said the Trump administration had made clear that "we are transitioning ​to provide critical, more limited support with allies in the lead.""President Trump has also been quite rightly and clearly frustrated with certain allies' behavior in recent months. So there's clearly at least some demand signal to have options that would show us (downgrading) our force levels in Europe," the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter.Still, the official said the review sought to "provide a spectrum of options from where we are to wherever" the review leads.Hegseth accuses some NATO allies of 'free-riding'Announcing the review in June, Hegseth chided some "free-riding" NATO allies and said the review would ensure US military "access, basing, and overflight are clearly delineated."The Terms of Reference go further.Beyond calling for reliable US access, basing and overflight rights, called ‌ABO, in allied NATO nations, they examine space, cyber and "intelligence architectures and infrastructure that enable US global power projection," the document says.The Pentagon expanded the definition of ABO to ensure the US takes into account all the types of support that NATO allies provide, the senior official said.The Terms ​of Reference also address ​other ways allies will be evaluated, and appear to ⁠be in line with previous US remarks by senior officials.The document says the Pentagon will seek to determine whether allies have a credible path to meet their NATO spending pledges and fill in gaps to NATO crisis forces - known as the NATO Force Model - after US reductions were announced earlier this year.Reuters has reported on a US questionnaire ​sent to allies to inform the review. It covers issues ranging from defense spending to strategy, procurement and support for US foreign policy priorities."What if any restrictions has the country placed on US access, basing, and overflight (ABO)? If so, why? Are they willing to reduce or eliminate any such restrictions?" the US asked in its questionnaire."Has the country publicly opposed regulations or other measures designed to inhibit or reduce transatlantic defense industrial cooperation? If so, how? If not, would they be willing to do so?" another question read.The responses are due by Friday."We are working very, very hard, and it is a relatively tight timeline," the official said. "A lot of prior analysis will inform this, which should allow us to move quicker on our end."Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Trump Claims Dolly Parton ‘Really Liked Me,' She Just Didn't Want Anyone To Know
news.text:
President Donald Trump reacted to news of Dolly Parton’s death by claiming that the country music icon secretly “really liked me” and that her death feels like losing “a member of the family.”

“I knew her a little bit, she wasn’t a very political person,” he said in an interview with Glenn Beck on Wednesday, a day after the “Jolene” singer-songwriter’s death sent shockwaves around the world.

“She really liked me, I will tell you,” he went on, while claiming she never expressed this publicly because she didn’t want to lose some of her fanbase.

“She was of the opinion, the 50%, who needs to lose?” he said. “I don’t think it’s 50, I think it’s probably 20% of the fans, OK, not 50. But she was a great person, just a nice person. I liked her a lot.”

In her memory, Trump ordered the nation’s flags to be flown at half mast for one week, one of the longest periods of national mourning ever issued for a private citizen.

“There has never been anyone like her, and never will,” he proclaimed in a social media post.

Parton had refused to publicly wade into politics, including by sharing her feelings about Trump. The businesswoman and philanthropist reasoned she didn’t want to offend anyone and divide her fans. She’d instead let her music ― and actions ― speak for her, she said.

“I know whatever I say, people are going to listen, and they’re going to make more of it than maybe what I meant. So I have to be careful. Of course I have my opinion, but I’m not an opinionated person as a rule,” she told People in 2021.

Some of the issues she did address and supported included equality for the LGBTQ+ community, children’s education and literacy, and vaccinations during the COVID-19 pandemic — with her having helped fund Moderna’s COVID-19 vaccine.

The Trump administration, in contrast, has increasingly advocated against vaccinations, with Trump appointing Robert F. Kennedy Jr., a long-time anti-vaxxer, to oversee the nation’s health department, leading to a historic rise in measles cases and unsupported claims that the shots may be linked to autism.

Trump also revoked executive orders and actions that called for nondiscrimination protections for LGBTQ+ individuals in federal agencies and in schools. His administration also carried out targeted campaigns against transgender individuals in schools, athletics and in the military.

“I think everybody should be treated with respect,” Dolly told CNN in 2016 when asked about a contentious anti-LGBTQ “Bathroom Bill” in North Carolina that imposed rules on bathroom and changing facilities based on one’s gender at birth.

“I don’t judge people. I try not to get too caught up in the controversy of things. I hope that everybody gets a chance to be who and what they are. I just know if I have to pee, I’m going to pee. I don’t care where it’s going to be,” she went on.

That same year, before elected into his first term, Trump said he agreed with trans individuals being allowed to use the bathroom of their choice. After being sworn in, his administration ended federal protections for transgender students.

news.title: Canada could use 2 key exports as leverage against Trump. One premier says that's a bad idea.
news.text: Canada is escalating its response to President Donald Trump's trade war, with another round of retaliatory tariffs set to take effect September 8. But two key Canadian exports — oil and potash, a key fertilizer ingredient — should stay out of the fight, one Canadian premier said Wednesday. "What we as a province cannot and will not support is any kind of export tariff on our natural resources or any of our resources that are being exported to the US or through the US to other areas of the world," said Scott Moe, the premier of Saskatchewan in Western Canada, at a press briefing. His warning comes as the US-Canada trade fight escalates. Trade negotiations broke down last week, and new 50% US tariffs on about $20 billion of Canadian imports took effect Saturday. On Monday, Trump threatened to raise tariffs on Canadian-made vehicles, auto parts, and steel to 50% beginning January 1, 2027. Canada is planning for dollar-for-dollar retaliation beginning September 8. On Tuesday, the country announced tariffs on 27.6 billion Canadian dollars, or about $20 billion, of US imports, including steel, dairy, and electronics. Canadian leaders have increasingly been looking for leverage over the US, from reconsidering F-35 purchases and targeting US coal shipments to raising the possibility of cutting off electricity exports. Moe said he supports Ottawa's targeted countertariffs, provided they limit the damage at home. "We are supportive of these very targeted countermeasures," he said, provided they have "a minimal impact on Canadian industries and families" and a larger effect on the US. But taxing potash exports would backfire by costing Canadian jobs and pushing US buyers toward other suppliers, he said. Canada is the world's largest potash exporter, accounting for about 40% of global exports in 2024, according to data from the Canadian government. The US received 53% of Canada's potash shipments that year. Oil is another red line for Moe. "We cannot in any way support the adding of export tariffs on a product like oil," he said, calling such a move "an unsustainable hit to our Canadian economy." The White House exempted energy and potash from its latest 50% tariffs. Moe said he has not heard Ottawa propose export tariffs on either commodity. He warned against retaliatory measures that might feel satisfying but ultimately hurt Canada's interests. "We should be very careful with respect to policies that maybe make us feel good at the moment," Moe said, arguing that the focus should instead be on measures that help get the US back to the negotiating table. Saskatchewan is retaliating elsewhere. Starting September 8, the province will impose a 50% levy on American alcohol while continuing to sell US booze. Canada is one of the US's largest trading partners, with about $870 billion in goods and services traded between the two countries in 2025.
news.summary: Canadian leaders are looking for leverage over the US, from F-35 purchases and coal shipments to cutting off electricity exports.

news.title: Trump Threatens New Trade War And Canada’s Carney Says Sure, Bring It On
news.text:
Six months after starting a real war he cannot figure out how to get out of, President Donald Trump has started another, potentially equally disastrous conflict: a trade war with America’s neighbour and second-largest partner.

And just as Iran is showing little interest in helping Trump out of his bind by agreeing to a face-saving deal that would let him claim victory, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is uninterested in letting Trump back away from the fight he began within weeks of returning to office.

Indeed, when Trump declared that he would impose even more tariffs on Canadian goods starting in January – two months after the midterm elections – Carney upped the ante and said no: His retaliatory tariffs would begin the day after Labor Day, the traditional start of the fall election campaign season.

“You’re at war when you’re attacked, and we got attacked,” Carney said in a weekend press conference explaining why he broke off trade negotiations.

He then said out loud what many US allies have believed for two years: that the United States under Trump is no longer a trustworthy partner. “We recognise that sometimes its signature was written in pencil.”

Trump’s new tariffs on a hodgepodge of goods from Canada will raise prices for US consumers even further in the run-up to the November elections, while Canadian tariffs will hurt US exporters who count on that business. Trump has also upped his volume of insults against Canada, claiming, for example, that he will rename Lake Ontario as Lake America.

Scott Lincicome, a trade analyst at the Cato Institute, said Trump chose to tangle with someone whose country is fully behind him.

“He’s a smart guy and it helps a lot that Canadians overwhelmingly hate Trump and will endure significant trade war pain to fight him,” he said.

Carney is not the first leader to say no to Trump. Mexican president Claudia Sheinbaum has rejected Trump’s demand to let him use US troops against suspected drug dealers in Mexico, criticised the weapons pipeline that sees high-powered guns enter her nation illegally from the US and stood up for Cuba as Trump effectively imposed a blockade — but has done these things relatively quietly.

Danish prime minister Mette Frederiksen has similarly refused to countenance Trump’s demand that her nation turn over Greenland.

Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni essentially called Trump a liar when he claimed she had begged to be photographed with him, while French president Emmanuel Macron chastised Trump for constantly saying contradictory things about Iran, even advising him to remain silent once in a while.

Carney ― whose doctorate in economics and former directorship at two central banks stand in stark contrast with Trump’s casino-bankrupting history in business ― is the first leader of a close ally to confront Trump head-on in a major dispute.

At that press conference, he pointed out a fact that has gotten glossed over in virtually all discussion of Trump’s tariffs against Canada since he retook office: they violate the 2020 congressionally-approved free trade update that Trump continually boasted about at the time.

“That’s the thing: We have a deal with the Americans. It’s called CUSMA,” he said, referring to what the US calls the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, essentially a renaming of the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement.

“We have side letters that clarify behaviour in steel, in aluminum, in autos. All of those are being violated, day in, day out.”

Trump does not, in his public comments, explain how Canada is cheating the United States under a trade agreement that he himself negotiated and signed. His White House press office said he is permitted under the agreement to impose tariffs on Canada to address emergencies and national security concerns, although it is unclear how Canada is causing either.

As with so many other things, Trump’s decision to act against Canada is rooted in his profound ignorance, in this case his longstanding inability to understand how international trade works.

For decades, Trump has claimed, falsely, that countries that sell more products to the United States than buy from the US are “ripping off” Americans. He further conflates trade deficits with the US budget deficit.

Trump’s first-term national security adviser, John Bolton, who, like many of Trump’s critics, has been criminally prosecuted by Trump’s Department of Justice, said the true workings of trade and tariffs were explained to Trump by experts in his own administration. “Many times,” he said.

Trump nevertheless repeated his falsehood again on Wednesday in a podcast appearance.

“We lose $60 billion a year, and really more than that, $60 billion a year with Canada,” he told former Fox News host Glenn Beck.

That view ignores the reality that Americans use and benefit from lumber, aluminium, maple syrup and other products they pay for. The trade imbalance, according to economists, is as meaningful as a typical family’s “trade deficit” each year with their neighbourhood grocery store.

Carney, in his news conference, told reporters that even by that metric, Trump is wrong because he fails to include services provided to Canadians by US companies that generate a net trade surplus for the United States. He further pointed out that much of the imports coming from Canada are natural gas, electricity and the heavy crude needed by many Texas refineries.

“I don’t think they want us to stop sending any of that energy,” he said.

That Carney has emerged as Trump’s biggest antagonist among traditional allies is perhaps unsurprising, given that his Liberal Party unexpectedly retained power in 2025 thanks to anti-Trump backlash among the Canadian populace after he returned to office and began talking about annexing Canada as the 51st state.

Carney provided a hint of where he stood in his speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, early this year.

“If great powers abandon even the pretense of rules and values for the unhindered pursuit of their power and interests, the gains from transactionalism will become harder to replicate,” he warned, clearly referring to the United States without ever mentioning Trump by name. “Hegemons cannot continually monetize their relationships.”

The end result of Trump’s tariff attacks and Carney’s retaliation is that residents in both countries will suffer, Bolton said.

“This is just going to hurt both economies. Trump raises taxes on Americans and Carney retaliates by raising taxes on Canadians,” he said.

news.title: Ukraine-Russia war latest: Trump issues first comment on CIA chief’s mysterious visit to Moscow
news.text:
US president Donald Trump has said “something may come out of” the CIA director John Ratcliffe’s visit to Moscow on Tuesday.

Trump said the US is “working very hard” to end the war in Ukraine, calling the CIA chief a “fantastic guy”.

Answering a question on Ratcliffe’s visit to Russia, Trump said that the CIA director made a visit to Russia on a “very semi-routine” basis and “something may come out of it”.

The Kremlin revealed yesterday that CIA director Ratcliffe held talks with Russian intelligence officials during a mysterious visit this week but did not meet president Vladimir Putin.

Spokesperson Dmitry Peskov framed communication between the two countries’ intelligence agencies as positive.

This comes as Kremlin sources said Russia is considering stepping up its ballistic missile strikes on Kyiv.

Putin is contemplating hitting targets in the city centre and on critical infrastructure elsewhere in Ukraine, after concluding that efforts to negotiate a peace deal have reached a dead end, they said.
news.summary: Trump says he is hopeful 'something may come out of' CIA chief’s meetings in Russia
news.author: Arpan Rai
